source_lines.27: **Graph convention.** For any finite real column-stochastic matrix $P$ on $S=\{1,\ldots,n\}$, the positive-transition graph has a directed edge $j\to i$ exactly when $P_{ij}>0$. This defines the communicating classes and closed classes for real matrices, whether or not their entries can be computed exactly.
source_lines.31: **Output.** A partition of $S$ into the strongly connected components of the directed graph of positive transitions, the list of closed communicating classes, and the remaining transient states.
source_lines.33: **Procedure.** Form the usual row-transition matrix $K=P^{\mathsf T}$. Initialize a Boolean relation $R_{ij}$ to true exactly when $i=j$ or $K_{ij}>0$. For $k=1,\ldots,n$, and then for every $i,j$, replace $R_{ij}$ by $R_{ij}\lor(R_{ik}\land R_{kj})$. Place $i,j$ in the same component exactly when both $R_{ij}$ and $R_{ji}$ are true. Mark a component $C$ closed exactly when $K_{ij}=0$ for every $i\in C$ and $j\notin C$. Return the closed components, the nonclosed components, and their state labels in increasing order. The procedure uses finitely many exact comparisons and Boolean updates; no sparse storage format or cost bound is asserted. It is a graph computation under the exact-comparison interface, not a claim that positivity of arbitrary unrepresented real numbers can be decided from rounded approximations.

source_lines.32: Fix a finite horizon $T>0$ and a nondegenerate fixed size interval $[0,X]$ with $X>0$. Let $g,\mu,\gamma:[0,X]\to[0,\infty)$ be bounded Lipschitz functions, with $g(x)\ge g_{\min}>0$. Here $g$ is size growth, $\mu$ is ordinary mortality, and $\gamma$ is the rate at which a dividing parent is removed. For each parent size $y\in[0,X]$, let $K_y$ be a finite nonnegative Borel measure of daughter sizes, supported on $[0,y]$. source_lines.38: The unit circle is an orbitally asymptotically stable periodic orbit of period $2\pi$. At $x_*=(1,0)$ the affine phase $\psi_b(x,y)=x-1$ has a singular phase-bordered shooting Jacobian, while $\psi_g(x,y)=y$ is transverse and gives an invertible phase-bordered shooting Jacobian.
source_lines.50: 1.1 The identities $\dot r=(xx'+yy')/r$ and $\dot\vartheta=(xy'-yx')/r^2$ give $\dot r=r(1-r)$ and $\dot\vartheta=1$. Thus $r=1$ is invariant and $\vartheta(t)=\vartheta(0)+t$, so the least period is $2\pi$. Differentiating $r(1-r)$ at $r=1$ gives the radial variational equation $\dot\rho=-\rho$, whose multiplier is $e^{-2\pi}<1$; the angular variational equation is $\dot\alpha=0$, whose multiplier is $1$. Because the polar-coordinate Jacobian at times $0$ and $2\pi$ is the same invertible matrix, the Cartesian monodromy is conjugate to $\operatorname{diag}(e^{-2\pi},1)$. For $r<1$ the radial derivative is positive, and for $r>1$ it is negative, so each nearby radius moves monotonically toward $1$ and remains between its initial value and $1$. It has a limit $\bar r$; if $\bar r(1-\bar r)\ne0$, then $\dot r=r(1-r)$ is eventually bounded away from zero, contradicting convergence. Let $g(t,x)=0$ be its $C^1$ guard, let $R(t,x)$ be its $C^1$ reset, and write $f^-=f_{m^-}(\tau,x^-)$ and $f^+=f_{m^+}(\tau,R(\tau,x^-))$. For event-time variations to the left of $\tau$, impose the same tube hypothesis on the time-reversed incoming field. source_lines.53: 1.1 Let $H(s,x)=g(s,\phi^-(s;\tau,x))$, where $\phi^-$ is the incoming mode flow initialized at the nominal pre-event time. The stated common-tube hypothesis and [F4], applied to the field and to its time reversal on the left interval, give the required $C^1$ flow dependence near $(\tau,x^-)$. By [F5], $H$ is $C^1$. At $(s,x)=(\tau,x^-)$, [F2] gives $\partial_sH=\kappa\ne0$. By [F3], the nearby event time $s=\tau(x)$ is $C^1$. Since $\phi^-(\tau;\tau,x)=x$, its initial-state derivative at $s=\tau$ is the identity. Implicit differentiation gives $D\tau(x^-)=-D_xg/\kappa$. Thus the actual shift $\delta\tau:=\tau_\delta-\tau$ satisfies $\delta\tau=-D_xg\,\delta x^-/\kappa+o(\|\delta x^-\|_2)$. [given, F2, F3, F4, F5, algebra]
source_lines.55: 2.1 At the perturbed event, [F4] gives incoming state $x^-+\delta x^-+f^-\delta\tau+o(\|\delta x^-\|_2)$. By [F5], the reset-state variation is $D_xR\,\delta x^-+(D_xR f^-+\partial_tR)\delta\tau+o(\|\delta x^-\|_2)$. Compare at $t_0=\max\{\tau,\tau+\delta\tau\}$. If $\delta\tau\ge0$, the nominal outgoing state advances from $\tau$ to $t_0$ by $f^+\delta\tau+o(|\delta\tau|)$, while the perturbed state has just reset. If $\delta\tau<0$, the perturbed outgoing state advances from its reset at $\tau+\delta\tau$ to $t_0=\tau$ by $f^+(-\delta\tau)+o(\|\delta x^-\|_2)$, while the nominal state has just reset. In both cases the same-clock difference is $D_xR\,\delta x^-+(D_xR f^-+\partial_tR-f^+)\delta\tau+o(\|\delta x^-\|_2)$, since step 1.1 gives $\delta\tau=O(\|\delta x^-\|_2)$. [given, F1, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]
